# Overview of this FAQ and how to get help

This is a list of some frequently asked questions (FAQ) on the GSVA package,
with answers and links to the relevant documentation and resources. If you have
any other question that you would like to see it included in this FAQ, please
open an [issue](https://github.com/rcastelo/GSVA/issues) in the GSVA GitHub
repo. Aside from this FAQ and opening a GitHub issue, you can also get help on
the GSVA package by:

1. Using the help system in R, e.g. `?gsva` or `help(gsva)`, and reading the
   package vignettes, which can be accessed from your own software installation
   with `browseVignettes("GSVA")`, or through the Bioconductor landing page for
   the GSVA package at https://bioconductor.org/packages/GSVA.

2. Posting your question on the
   [Bioconductor support site](https://support.bioconductor.org), please make
   sure you have read first the
   [Bioconductor posting guide](https://bioconductor.org/help/support/posting-guide).

# How do I cite GSVA

If you use the GSVA package in your research, please cite the following paper:

[@haenzelmann2013gsva]: Hänzelmann, Sonja, Robert Castelo, and Justin Guinney. 2013. “GSVA: Gene Set Variation Analysis for Microarray and RNA-Seq Data.” _BMC Bioinformatics_ 14: 7. https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2105-14-7.

Additionally, if you use any of the following methods implemented in the GSVA
package, please cite the corresponding papers:

  * _ssgsea_ [@barbie_systematic_2009]: Barbie, David A., Pablo Tamayo, Jesse S. Boehm, So Young Kim, Susan E. Moody, Ian F. Dunn, Anna C. Schinzel, et al. 2009. “Systematic RNA Interference Reveals That Oncogenic KRAS-driven Cancers Require TBK1.” _Nature_ 462 (7269): 108–12. https://doi.org/10.1038/nature08460.

  * _zscore_ [@lee_inferring_2008]: Lee, Eunjung, Han-Yu Chuang, Jong-Won Kim, Trey Ideker, and Doheon Lee. 2008. “Inferring Pathway Activity Toward Precise Disease Classification.” _PLOS Computational Biology_ 4:e1000217. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1000217.

  * _plage_ [@tomfohr_pathway_2005]: Tomfohr, John, Jun Lu, and Thomas B Kepler. 2005. “Pathway Level Analysis of Gene Expression Using Singular Value Decomposition.” _BMC Bioinformatics_ 6:225. https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2105-6-225.

# Common error messages and how to fix them

## There is no package called 'GSVA'

If you encounter the error:

```{sh, eval=FALSE}
Error in library(GSVA) : there is no package called 'GSVA'
```
This is because the GSVA package is not installed. You can install it with:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
    install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install("GSVA")
```

## Could not find function "gsva"

If you encounter the error:

```{sh, eval=FALSE}
Error in gsva() : could not find function "gsva"
```
This is because the GSVA package is not loaded. You can load it with:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
library(GSVA)
```

## Unable to find an inherited method for function ‘gsva’ for signature

If you encounter one of the following two errors:

```{sh, eval=FALSE}
Error in gsva(): Calling gsva(expr=., gset.idx.list=., method=., ...) is defunct

[... or ...]

Error: unable to find an inherited method for function ‘gsva’ for signature ‘param = "matrix"’
```
where the last part could also be `param = "SummarizedExperiment"`,
`param = "SingleCellExperiment"`, `param = "SpatialExperiment"`, etc., this is
because you are providing a wrong first argument in the call to `gsva()`. In
versions < 1.50 (up to October 2023, Bioconductor release 3.17), this first
argument was the object containing the input expression data. However, starting
with version 1.50 (October 2023, Bioconductor release 3.18), the first argument
should be an object of class `GsvaMethodParam` built with a constructor function
according to the method you want to use, e.g. `gsvaParam()`, `ssgseaParam()`,
`zscoreParam()`, or `plageParam()`. See the first
[GSVA package vignette](https://bioconductor.org/packages/GSVA) for more details
and examples.

## No identifiers in the gene sets could be matched to the identifiers in the expression data

If you encounter the error:

```{sh, eval=FALSE}
No identifiers in the gene sets could be matched to the identifiers in the expression data
```
It means that none of the identifiers in your gene sets could be matched to the
identifiers in your expression data. This is usually because the identifiers in
your gene sets are of a different type than the identifiers in your expression
data, and both input expression and gene sets lack the necessary metadata to
map one type onto the other. For example, your gene sets may contain gene
symbols, while your expression data may contain Ensembl gene IDs. You can check
whether the annotation metadata is present in your input expression data by
typing `gsvaAnnotation(expr)`, where `expr` is your input expression data. If
the output is `NULL`, it means that the annotation metadata is missing. In such
a case, you can add it with:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
library(GSEABase)

gsvaAnnotation(expr) <- xxxxIndentifier("org.Xx.eg.db")
```
where `xxxxIdentifier` is the appropriate function for the type of identifiers
in your expression data, e.g. `ENSEMBLIdentifier()`, `EntrezIdentifier()`, etc..
Note that you should load the package
[GSEABase](https://bioconductor.org/packages/GSEABase) to use these functions,
and you may obtain help about them by typing `help(GeneIdentifierType)`. Here
also`org.Xx.eg.db` is the appropriate organism-level annotation package for your
expression data, e.g. `org.Hs.eg.db` for human, `org.Mm.eg.db` for mouse, etc.
Please check the
[Bioconductor annotation packages](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/BiocViews.html#___AnnotationData)
for the available organism-level annotation packages.

You can also check whether the annotation metadata is present in your gene sets
by typing `gsvaAnnotation(gsets)`, where `gsets` is the object containing your
input gene sets. If the output is `NULL`, it means that the annotation metadata
is missing. In such a case, if `gsets` is a `list` object, you can add the
annotation metadata in the same way as for the input expression data.

# GSVA scores

## How should the input expression data be pre-processed before running GSVA?

Our recommendation is to pre-process the input expression data in the same way
as you would do for a differential expression analysis, i.e. removing lowly
expressed genes and normalizing the columns of expression data to reduce
technical biases, such as differences in sequencing depth and RNA composition.
GSVA does not read normalization factors or offsets produced by some
normalization pipelines and associated with raw integer counts, so it is
necessary to use those factors or offsets to transform the intput raw integer
counts into normalized continuous units of expression, such as log2 CPM, or
log2 TPM.

## Why GSVA scores differ with respect to previous versions of the GSVA package?

The GSVA package includes _regression_ tests that are routinely run in the
Bioconductor [build system](https://bioconductor.org/checkResults) and which are
used to detect unintended changes in the GSVA scores with respect to previous
versions of the package, caused by, e.g., bugs or new features. So, in
principle, given the same input, GSVA scores should not differ with respect to
previous versions of the package. However, this still could happen in the
following cases:

1. One or more of the input gene sets contain duplicated gene identifiers
   within a gene set. Albeit uncommon, such duplicated gene identifiers could
   be already present in the input gene sets, but more often they can be
   introduced when mapping the identifiers in the input gene sets to a different
   type of identifiers, e.g. when two gene symbols map to the same Ensembl gene
   identifier. In previous versions of the GSVA package, such duplicated
   identifiers were not detected and were included in the calculations, wrongly
   biasing them. In the current version of GSVA such duplicated identifiers are
   detected and removed before the calculations, leading to a GSVA score for
   such a gene set that may differ with respect to previous versions of the
   package.
2. In single-cell or spatially resolved transcriptomics data, zero values in
   gene sets were treated differently in previous versions of the GSVA package,
   leading to different GSVA scores. In the current version of GSVA, zero values
   in gene sets are treated in a particular way that makes GSVA scores stable.
   In this type of data, the default row-normalization method has also changed,
   to a more performant method (CLR). You can switch back to the previous method
   using the parameter `rowNorm` in the call to `gsvaParam()`. Please consult
   `help(gsvaParam)` and the vignette on using GSVA with single-cell data.
3. If you use GPU acceleration, GSVA scores may differ with respect to previous
   versions of the GSVA package because the calculations are performed in single
   precision, please consult the vignette on using GSVA with GPU hardware.

## How do I interpret GSVA scores and fold changes between them?

A positive GSVA score for a given gene set in a given column means that the
genes that form that gene set tend to occur towards the top of the ranking of
decreasing expression values of that column. A negative one means that those
genes in the gene set tend to occur towards the bottom of that ranking. A GSVA
score close to zero means that those genes in the gene set do not show any
preference towards the top or the bottom of that ranking.

In the way that GSVA scores are derived, the magnitude of a fold change or
difference in means between two groups of columns for a given gene set is
difficult to interpret, but you can interpret the direction (over-expression
or under-expression of that gene set or pathway) and test with linear models
whether a coefficient derived from GSVA scores is significantly different from
zero; see subsection on differential expression at pathway level of the first
[GSVA vignette](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/GSVA/inst/doc/GSVA.html#72_Differential_expression_at_pathway_level)
and the GSVA publication [@haenzelmann2013gsva] for further details.

## Why are some of the GSVA scores negative?

A GSVA score for a given gene set in a given column is negative when the
expression levels of the genes in that gene set rank lower than the expression
levels of the genes outside that gene set in that column. The function
`gsvaEnrichment()` can be used to produce an enrichment plot that helps to
understand how the GSVA score was calculated. Please also consult the
GSVA publication [@haenzelmann2013gsva] for more details on how the GSVA scores
are calculated.

# ssGSEA scores

## Why ssGSEA scores differ with respect to previous versions of the GSVA package?

The GSVA package includes _regression_ tests that are routinely run in the
Bioconductor [build system](https://bioconductor.org/checkResults) and which are
used to detect unintended changes in the ssGSEA scores with respect to previous
versions of the package, caused by, e.g., bugs or new features. So, in
principle, given the same input, ssGSEA scores should not differ with respect to
previous versions of the package. However, this still could happen when one or
more of the input gene sets contain duplicated gene identifiers within a gene
set. Albeit uncommon, such duplicated gene identifiers could be already present
in the input gene sets, but more often they can be introduced when mapping the
identifiers in the input gene sets to a different type of identifiers, e.g. when
two gene symbols map to the same Ensembl gene identifier. In previous versions
of the GSVA package, such duplicated identifiers were not detected and were
included in the calculations, wrongly biasing them. In the current version of
GSVA such duplicated identifiers are detected and removed before the
calculations, leading to a ssGSEA score for such a gene set that may differ with
respect to previous versions of the package.

## Are ssGSEA scores different between its GSVA implementation and the implementation by the Broad Institute?

The implementation of ssGSEA in the GSVA package is based on the original
publication by Barbie et al. [@barbie_systematic_2009], and in principle the
resulting enrichment scores should be nearly identical to the scores obtained
with the first implementation by the authors of that publication, at the Broad
Institute, available at https://github.com/GSEA-MSigDB/ssGSEA-gpmodule, and as
the _ssGSEAProjection module_ in the
[GenePattern](https://www.genepattern.org/modules/docs/ssGSEAProjection/4)
software. There have been subsequent versions of the ssGSEA algorithm by
the Broad Institute,
[ssGSEA 2.0](https://github.com/broadinstitute/ssGSEA2.0) and
[ssGSEA 3.0](https://github.com/broadinstitute/ssGSEA3.0), which are not
implemented in the GSVA package.

# PLAGE scores

## Why PLAGE scores differ with respect to previous versions of the GSVA package?

The GSVA package includes _regression_ tests that are routinely run in the
Bioconductor [build system](https://bioconductor.org/checkResults) and which are
used to detect unintended changes in the PLAGE scores with respect to previous
versions of the package, caused by, e.g., bugs or new features. So, in
principle, given the same input, PLAGE scores should not differ with respect to
previous versions of the package. However, this still could happen in the
following cases:

1. One or more of the input gene sets contain duplicated gene identifiers
   within a gene set. Albeit uncommon, such duplicated gene identifiers could
   be already present in the input gene sets, but more often they can be
   introduced when mapping the identifiers in the input gene sets to a different
   type of identifiers, e.g. when two gene symbols map to the same Ensembl gene
   identifier. In previous versions of the GSVA package, such duplicated
   identifiers were not detected and were included in the calculations, wrongly
   biasing them. In the current version of GSVA such duplicated identifiers are
   detected and removed before the calculations, leading to a PLAGE score for
   such a gene set that may differ with respect to previous versions of the
   package.
2. The sign of PLAGE scores may change with respect to earlier versions of GSVA,
   since instead of being the arbitrary default of the SVD, it is now set so
   that scores correlate positively with the mean expression of the gene set.

# Z-scores

## Why Z-scores differ with respect to previous versions of the GSVA package?

The GSVA package includes _regression_ tests that are routinely run in the
Bioconductor [build system](https://bioconductor.org/checkResults) and which are
used to detect unintended changes in the Z-scores with respect to previous
versions of the package, caused by, e.g., bugs or new features. So, in
principle, given the same input, Z-scores should not differ with respect to
previous versions of the package. However, this still could happen when one or
more of the input gene sets contain duplicated gene identifiers within a gene
set. Albeit uncommon, such duplicated gene identifiers could be already present
in the input gene sets, but more often they can be introduced when mapping the
identifiers in the input gene sets to a different type of identifiers, e.g. when
two gene symbols map to the same Ensembl gene identifier. In previous versions
of the GSVA package, such duplicated identifiers were not detected and were
included in the calculations, wrongly biasing them. In the current version of
GSVA such duplicated identifiers are detected and removed before the
calculations, leading to a Z-score for such a gene set that may differ with
respect to previous versions of the package.

# Large input expression datasets

## Can I run GSVA on a large input expression dataset that does not fit into main memory?

Yes, as long as it is stored in HDF5 format with the proper layout. If the
dataset is sparse, such as those produced by single-cell and spatially resolved
transcriptomics, substantial performance gains can be obtained when the HDF5
layout of the file only stores nonzero values as a compressed sparse column
(CSC) matrix (e.g., [10x Genomics HDF5](https://www.10xgenomics.com/support/software/cell-ranger-arc/latest/analysis/outputs/outputs-h5-matrices)).
With default parameters, GSVA will use 90% of the available main memory of the
computer to perform calculations. Memory consumption can be controlled with the
parameter `maxmem` in the calls to `gsva()`, `gsvaRowNorm()`, `gsvaColRanks()`
and `gsvaColScores()`.

## Can I run GSVA calculations in parallel in my computer?

Yes, using the `BPPARAM` parameter in the calls to `gsva()`, `gsvaRowNorm()`,
`gsvaColRanks()`; please consult the details on that parameter in the manual
pages of those functions.

## Can I run GSVA calculations in parallel in a high-performance computing cluster?

Yes, using the functions `gsvaMap()` and `gsvaReduce()`; please consult the
package vignette entitled
[Using GSVA on GPUs, HPC clusters and the cloud](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/GSVA/inst/doc/GSVA_GPU_HPC_cloud.html).

# Interoperability with other software ecosystems

## Seurat objects

You can convert a Seurat object into a `SingleCellExperiment` object with the
function `as.SingleCellExperiment()` from the CRAN package
[Seurat](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=Seurat), and then use that object
as input to the `gsva()` function.

## scverse AnnData objects

For AnnData objects version < 0.8.0, you can use the CRAN package
[anndata](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=anndata) and its function
`read_h5ad()` to convert an AnnData object into a `SingleCellExperiment` object.
If the `AnnData` object has version >= 0.8.0, you should use the Bioconductor
[anndataR](https://bioconductor.org/packages/anndataR), and its function
`read_h5ad()`. Please consult the documentation of those packages for more
details on how to use them.
